subsubtopic: REPORTING OF PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS ON CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, earlier this week the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) issued an open letter to all Canadians concerning the testing of the Cruise missile in Canada. While many of the comments I have seen have perverted the Prime Minister's letter, at least some of the print media published, along with their rather fallacious stories, the text of the Prime Minister's letter. That is not the case, however, with the comments made on the CBC "National News" last evening. Those comments were a total perversion of what the Prime Minister had to say. I think the Canadian public and Members of this House have a right to expect better than that from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I would hope, Madam Speaker, that the newscaster in future would read such documents before he makes fallacious, vicious and perverted comments about them. I hope we will see the estimates for the CBC separated from the general Government estimates in this House so we can vote on them separately and some of us can express to the CBC with our votes what we think of its perversion of truth.

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-EFFECT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON LIVESTOCK INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some 86 years ago the historic Crow rate was struck at one half cent per ton per mile to export grain from the Prairies. For some 70 years grain producers, the livestock industry, railway companies, and secondary processors all made money. However, during the last 16 years, primarily as a result of inflation, the Crow rate has caused an enormous distortion between the grain industry on one hand, and the
livestock industry and secondary processors on the other. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) appointed Mr. Clay Gilson who, with 12 commodity groups and approximately 60 or 70 people, came up with a phased solution which was balanced between the legitimate interests of the competing groups.
Then, Madam Speaker, politics became involved, which resulted in the Pepin compromise of last February. Then raw, ugly politics entered into it, which resulted in Bill C-155. That Bill is totally unacceptable to the livestock industry and is not in the long-term best interests of the nation. I call upon my colleagues opposite and in the NDP to make sure we do not write off that livestock industry because, if we do that to western Canada, we are going to cut off a lot of tax revenue for this part of the country.

subsubtopic: THE PARABLE OF THE FARMER AND THE PLUM TREE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to spend a little bit of time recounting a story, to make my point.
Some years ago a constituent of mine took over a farm after learning to become an experienced farm manager at university. He applied the most efficient methods known to man at that time, and ran the farm with a great deal of success. His First crop was a very good one at the lowest cost per unit produced for years.
At the end of the harvest he went walking around the farm to check out other things he could do to make the operation more efficient. He came across a little plum orchard that his father, and his sister who was a plant geneticist, had set up.
He noted that of the dozen trees in that orchard only nine had fruit on them. So, being very efficiency minded, he immediately went in with a tractor and pulled out the three that were not producing fruit. Since then there has been no fruit growing in that orchard. He killed the orchard because he pulled out the male trees.
I think this is what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is doing when he introduces a new Crow rate. He is looking at the hole, not the doughnut. He has missed the point entirely, and I urge him to change his mind.

May 11, 1983

subsubtopic: CATHOLIC CHURCHMEN'S VIEWS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one issue which has been receiving the attention of Conferences of Catholic Bishops globally is the moral implications of the controversial use of nuclear deterrence as a means of defence and as a means of promoting eventual arms reduction and peace. But the average practising Catholic is confused by the number of statements issued by Catholic leaders on the subject of nuclear arms.
A quick survey of decisions reached indicates that in Italy no directive or guidelines were issued by the Italian Conference of Bishops. In West Germany, Catholic Bishops published a pastoral letter condemning the arms race but upholding the right to use the threat of nuclear retaliation as a deterrent to war. They also condemned the expansionist aims of totalitarian states. The Roman Catholic Bishops of the United States, who have the support of the Canadian Bishops, condemned first strike use of nuclear weapons and condemned the targeting of nuclear weapons against civilian targets. They accept as moral the deployment of nuclear weapons as a deterrent, but not as a purpose in itself-only as a step toward progressive disarmament.
Pope John Paul II, in his message to the Second United Nations Special Session on Disarmament on June 11, 1982, said, "In current conditions, deterrence based on balance, certainly not as an end in itself but as a step towards progressive disarmament, may still be judged morally acceptable". subsubtopic: TAXABLE BENEFITS-TREATMENT OF ROAD WORKERS AND COMPANY EXECUTIVES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House another paradox involving taxable benefits under the Income Tax Act.
For some time in Nova Scotia, National Revenue has been questioning road foremen and other classes of employees of the provincial Department of Transportation in a dispute over the use of vehicles and rates of pay affecting taxable benefits, involving these employees.
On the other hand I have reason to believe that Massey-Ferguson, the beneficiary of many millions of dollars of taxpayers' money for loan guarantees, which the Government had to pay, rewarded certain of its executives for their success in negotiating benefits for their company from the Government. The rewards apparently consisted, in some instances, of trips abroad for these people and their families, in lieu of
bonuses. Has Massey-Ferguson been audited in this respect? Have any of these executives been audited, or indeed, have any of the executives included these benefits as part of their taxable incomes?
If not, we have two standards-a very strict one affecting many workers in Nova Scotia who are relatively low income people, while this company, which may be closer to an Edsel than a Chrysler success story, although I hope not, may be playing fast and loose with the tax system. I would appreciate it if the Minister would check into this situation.

subsubtopic: TESTING OF CHEMICAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as most Canadians are now aware, the Liberal-Conservative coalition of the right is in support of testing the Cruise missile and other nuclear technologies on Canadian soil.
Just as insidious is the recent decision by the Liberals to test H-16 at McGill University in Montreal, this year. This chemical is undergoing tests on dogs, rats, and pigs and, according to National Defence officials, it "would be used by our troops in the event that they are subjected to chemical attack".
The Geneva Convention, of which Canada is a signatory, is an international agreement prohibiting the practice of chemical warfare. Canadians would be naive to assume that the H-16 tests which are now under way at McGill University are being conducted solely for defence. Clearly, this synthetic replacement for atropine is being designed to respond to certain nerve gases and chemicals for use in warfare; most likely against civilian populations.
Perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would explain to Canadians just what Canada's role is in the field of chemical and biological warfare, and explain to the House what situations he foresees where Canadian troops will be in contact with chemicals requiring H-16 as an antidote. Perhaps the Prime Minister would also explain the $204,000 order for chemical air burst dispensers in February, or the $109,000 in March for chemical simulators, while he is at it.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS-DISAPPEARANCE OF JOBS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with the skill of Houdini, the Government has dazzled Canadian shipbuilders with promises of wonderful and amazing things to come. The shipbuilding policy announced last January was heralded by the Government as a program to save the Canadian shipbuilding industry. The Government has failed to produce even the slightest evidence it seriously intends to implement new policies that will be meaningful.
May 11, 1983

Two weeks ago the Government announced the Canadian Coast Guard Fleet Acquisition Program to modernize the aging Coast Guard fleet at a cost of $630 million over the next four years. It will be late June before any contracts are awarded, and Christmas before any work begins. In the meantime more jobs will have vanished from the Saint John shipyards and other shipyards across the nation.
The Canadian Patrol Frigate Program has been a mystical illusion. Shipbuilders have repeatedly urged the Government to move up the starting date of the Program. Delays in implementing the frigate program mean a needless loss of jobs.
Programs are being pulled from hats like rabbits, while jobs are disappearing quicker than you can say abracadabra. In 1981 some 1,627 people were employed at the Saint John shipyard; by Christmas the shipyard is expected to be a graveyard if the Government's programs fail to materalize.
Canadian shipbuilders are saying, "Quit the hocus-pocus and the shell games. Implement a new shipbuilding policy, spread the Coast guard work fairly throughout the country, and accelerate the frigate program." Shipbuilders want jobs- not another performance of the Government's magic show.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) betrayed the national voluntary organizations.
The Minister of Finance consulted with the voluntary organizations before his budget, and then betrayed them in his budget. The national volunteers requested that a 50 per cent cent tax credit replace the standard $100 deduction for charitable donations, but the Minister did not comply. He removed the $100 standard deduction only, thus hurting the thousands of people who donate to Poppy Day and Daffodil Day, where no receipts are given; hurting the thousands of hard-working volunteers who do work that the Government would otherwise have to do.
The removal of the standard deduction increases the administrative costs and mailing costs. In fact, Canada Post is about the only winner. It perpetrates the inequities in the tax treatment of charitable donations and fails to provide a stimulus needed by voluntary organizations. It is a slap in the face to the national voluntary organizations.
I urge the Minister to introduce the tax credit now or, at the very least, keep the $100 standard deduction until the entire proposal made by the voluntary organizations can be accepted.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY TO UPGRADE VETERINARY COLLEGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member knows that education is under provincial jurisdiction. We have previously entered into contracts with veterinary colleges to fund as high as 50 per cent of the cost of construction projects. I am sure he is also aware that the Government of Canada, through the Secretary of State, funds the operating costs of these schools. In Ontario, I believe the funding is approximately 59 per cent of the total cost.
For the last addition at Guelph, we funded $3 million of the construction cost. They made an agreement at that time that they would look after all of the costs involved for the next ten years, and would up the number of students to be educated from 80 to 120. They now say the school cannot do this. I have visited quite a few veterinary schools in different parts of the world. I would say that Guelph is up to the standard of any school in the world, and we will continue to do everything in our power to ensure that it continues to be so.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY TO UPGRADE VETERINARY COLLEGES
speechtext: I am well aware that veterinary colleges are under the jurisdiction of the respective Provinces and that the Provinces must as well pursue a more active role to turn this around.

Madam Speaker, I would ask the Minister whether he would take it upon himself to get the ball rolling and perhaps arrange meetings with his provincial counterparts along with the deans of the two colleges, taking whatever steps are necessary to rectify this whole matter which should never have been allowed to occur in the first place.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the president of the university has been at our office. We have also had meetings at Guelph about this. I had a discussion as recently as ten days ago with the provincial Minister of Agriculture. But if you will recall, it was because

May 11, 1983
Oral Questions
of the wisdom of someone in the Ontario Government that the veterinary college and agricultural school was taken away from the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture and put under the jurisdiction of the Minister of education in the Province of Ontario. The downgrading of the agricultural school began at that time.

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour and concerns women and part-time work. Seventy-two per cent of part-time workers are women. Most have low wages, no benefits, no pensions, and no job security. This kind of exploitation must stop.

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: I want to ask the Minister what changes he intends to make to the Labour Code to extend protection for all part-time workers who are under federal jurisdiction, and will he also remove the restrictions that deny part-time workers in the Government the right to unionize?

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we on this side of the House do not need to be lectured by the Hon. Member on the increased importance of part-time work and the effect it has on women. This is the reason why the Government has commissioned a study on this particular very important issue. The study ought to be ready for publication by Labour Canada in a matter of weeks, and when we have the recommendations contained in that study, which will become public very soon, as I mentioned, then we will be able to answer the Hon. Member's question specifically.
speakername: Hon.   Chas. L. Caccia@Minister of Labour

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: Certainly the Minister could make changes in his jurisdiction immediately. He does not need a study to do that.

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Employment. Many part-time workers and casual workers are not eligible for Unemployment Insurance benefits. Will the Minister amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to cover part-time workers and, in particular, will he change the minimum requirement for Unemployment Insurance to 100
hours of work over a ten-week period, which would help casual employees?

subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF PART-TIME WORKERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who undertook in committee the other night to make certain changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act regarding the discriminatory aspects that presently exists with regard to maternity leave. Could the Minister tell us when he would be prepared to introduce those changes which are so desperately needed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

I think the Hon. Member would recognize that what I said in committee was that if the Opposition, meaning her Party and those in the New Democratic Party, were prepared to give quick and immediate passage to those amendments along with others that are absolutely essential and are required to bring about the changes, the Government would look very favourably upon doing so, but we would need that assurance from the Hon. Member and her colleagues first.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Small Business. In the recent budget and in statements outside the House the Minister and others have commented on the changes that will occur to the Federal Business Development Bank. I ask the Minister if he could tell us how these changes will affect the access Canadian business people will have to the funds in the Federal Business Development Bank, what people will qualify for the equity position that the bank may now take, and whether people will be able to refinance under those provisions.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: BUSINESS PEOPLE'S ACCESS TO FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there was a similar discussion in the House a little while ago. Actually each case must obviously be judged on its own merits. With regard to taking an equity position, that would not be the preferred option. Obviously the preferred option is to let the private sector do its job, but if a case occurred where the only option seemed to be to take an equity position, then the Bank would do that with the understanding that it would get out as quickly as possible.
I might say that the new role of the Bank will be in venture capital, and I think that that is important for small business. We want to make this the small business bank, and we particularly want to make it the bank for the rural areas of Canada.

subtopic: INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO SMALL BUSINESSES
INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. If the Government is prepared to try to make it the bank for small business, is the Government also prepared to look at the interest rates that are being charged to some of those Canadian small businesses that are now financed by the Federal Business Development Bank, and is there any provision or undertaking by the Government to help relieve those businesses which are facing interest rates of up to 22 per cent over a long period of time, so that we can thus protect Canadian business and the jobs that that implies?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO SMALL BUSINESSES

Madam Speaker, obviously we would want to give the most favourable interest rates possible. The Hon. Member will note that last week we announced a certain
Oral Questions
reduction in the interest rates of the Federal Business Development Bank. I might say, though, that the reason for the higher rates is because, in most cases, the banks have been getting into very high risk situations. We do want to give every possible break to the small-businessman. I repeat that we want to make this a bank for small-businessmen, particularly for those in the rural areas of Canada where, in my opinion, the private sector has not always met the need.

I wonder if he can tell the House if there have been any further developments since that time, and can he assure the House that he will monitor them closely? It would appear that attitudes have not yet hardened, and if he would monitor the situation closely before it degenerates into a long-term interruption of services, as did EPA, he will do the region a great service.

speechtext:

May 11, 1983
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: NICARAGUA-INQUIRY RESPECTING POSSIBLE SOVIET INVOLVEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member that the Government is looking very closely at the situation in Central America. I think there have been some statements made about our interest there. The Prime Minister has expressed his views and concerns about the situation in Central America to President Reagan in Washington. We are receiving the usual information about what is going on in that part of the world. As far as the implication that other countries are delivering arms to that part of the world is concerned, I believe that it is public knowledge that there is much interference in these countries from one side or the other. As was stated before, I believe the policy of the Government is that Nicaragua should be run by Nicaraguans, and no other country should be involved in the internal affairs of this or any other country.

Member for Saskatoon East, asked the other day about the Contadora group's proposal-this is the proposal of the Contadora group which would encourage bilateral negotiations between Nicaragua and the United States, and bilateral negotiations between Nicaragua and Honduras-could the Prime Minister indicate whether the Canadian Government is going to give its support, as part of the requested international support, to the Contadora group's proposal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Public Works who, earlier in the Question Period, indicated that a young couple were grossly ill advised to give notice of vacating their apartment and entering into a purchase order for a new home, on the basis of what I thought was a reasonable expectation on their behalf of what was contained in the budget with respect to the $3,000 subsidy.
The other gross mistake which was brought to the attention of the House by the Minister was that the Government and Central Mortgage, despite the best advice available to it, grossly under-estimated the market. Given these two mistakes, one by a young couple hoping to purchase their first house, and the other by a Department which, according to the Minister possesses the best experts in the field, who, in the interest of
May 11, 1983

fairness and equity, in the Minister's view, should pay the price of that mistake?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: ENDING OF $3,000 GRANT PROGRAM-CONSEQUENCES FOR RENTER APPLICANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understood the previous Hon. Member to say that some people had given up their apartment as if they were just waiting to enter a house for which a foundation had not yet been laid. I thought that that sort of rhetoric did not help the debate.
I believe the question of the Hon. Member for Perth is a very serious one. Obviously, there are criteria which have to be met when you are applying for a $3,000 home ownership grant. Surely those, at least, should be met before major decisions, such as giving up an apartment, are made. On the other hand, I said that we had estimated, to the best of our knowledge, what would be the normal housing starts in the best years which we have seen in the housing history of the country. It is obvious that confidence has returned and a lot of Canadians want to build houses. There are a lot of savings which are not used and that is what we were trying to encourage.
I did not say so in my previous answers, but Canadians should also look at the other announcements made by the Minister of Finance, such as on the Registered Home Ownership Plan, which really offers considerable advantages in many cases. In fact some of them are superior to the $3,000 grant. That being said, I am assessing the size of the problem. As soon as I have information I will answer the serious question raised by the Hon. Member.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA EXPLORATION FOR OIL OFF CHINA COAST
PETRO-CANADA EXPLORATION FOR OIL OFF CHINA COAST
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. As the Minister will know, Petro-Canada has just announced that it is going to spend Canadian taxpayer dollars on off-shore exploration for oil off mainland China. The Minister will also know that Petro-Canada announced the closing of a project in northeastern Alberta related to the heavy oil sands. Can the Minister explain why, in this time of economic stagnation, when jobs are needed in Canada, we are spending, through Petro-Canada, Canadian dollars for jobs off mainland China, but withdrawing funds which are creating jobs in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA EXPLORATION FOR OIL OFF CHINA COAST

I believe this agreement with China is creating an opportunity in the field of oil and gas for drilling in an area where there is a great opportunity. In so far as the problems within Canada are
Oral Questions
concerned, we are working all the time on some projects. I am in constant touch with the Government of Alberta. We are trying to develop new projects. I think that to link the two projects the way the Hon. Member just did, is absoltely unfair and uncalled for.

Madam Speaker, I would disagree with the Minister that linking the two projects is not fair. I would like to remind the Minister that in northeastern Alberta the total known reserves in the tar sands and in the oil sands surpass all of the reserves in the Middle East. Is it not time that the Government looked to our own security of energy supply, of oil supply, and developed those resources, rather than move off to China and develop mainland China resources for their security of supply?

In terms of his comment on the energy situation in Canada, I invite him to read the comments of Total Petroleum, as reported in the press this morning, where they said that the only place they can do good business in oil at this time is in Canada.

subsubtopic: MR. MUNRO (ESQUIMALT-SAANICH)-PROCEDURE RESPECTING NOTIFICATION OF ITEMS FOR DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the proposer of the first motion but I feel my
Point of Order-Mr. Donald W. Munro
point of order is a matter which concerns all Members on Wednesdays, the timing of the notification of Bills or Motions or whatever is to be brought before us today.
The projected daily order of business reached my office at 11.10 today, Mr. Speaker. The notification which is published and photostated is not in our lobby. The one in the lobby now is the one placed there by our Deputy Whip for last week's proceedings. This is not good enough. There are matters brought before the House by Private Members which are important, not just to individual Members but to the country. We are here to bring forward for the consideration of this House matters which the Governments not prepared to consider. Members should have, and do have, the right to bring them forward. They should have the opportunity to prepare properly for their consideration.
The selection of subjects is also a very great mystery to everyone, Mr. Speaker. I understand there is a fair amount of telephoning to Members asking whether we are prepared to raise a particular matter, say, tomorrow. Perhaps they even call us on the same day the matter is to be brought forward. That selection process is not clear in anyone's mind.
I am sorry to eat into the time of the Hon. Member by ten minutes, not of the first speaker, but of the third matter to be considered today. His time will be reduced by ten minutes or by however long this point of order takes, unless there is unanimous consent of the House to do otherwise.
My contention, Mr. Speaker, is that the rules governing Private Members' Business are not clear. They are not sufficiently clarified in the Order Paper for everyone to receive sufficient notice-the proposer, for example-or for those who wish to speak to the matter to receive notice to prepare themselves. There is not sufficient time for each matter to be considered for an hour for the full three hours.
Those three matters deserve the most careful consideration by the Chair. All backbenchers are concerned and I think I am speaking for them in raising this point of order this afternoon.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of creating a Royal Commission on Maritime Industrial Opportunities for Canada with terms of reference to include studies and recommendations (a) on the feasibility and benefits of creating a Canadian merchant fleet (b) on co-ordinating the efforts of Government, industry and organized labour in creating a Canadian merchant fleet (c) on a course of action which would allow Canadians to identify and capture future economic benefits in the marine industrial sector, such as offshore mineral development and seabed mining.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion originally found itself on the Order Paper on November 26, 1981. It is rather interesting that we should be debating the motion today since some action has been taken to generate shipbuilding interest across the country. However, I still believe that this motion is relevant because what activity has been provided by the Government in this field is quite hopelessly inadequate when measured against the opportunities that are available for Canadians.
I think most Members of the House would recognize that the date of this motion comes after considerable and hard-fought debate on the Canada Oil and Gas Act, Bill C-48. In that Act the Government provided a number of measures which it claimed would provide industrial benefits to Canada from oil and gas development, particularly from offshore oil and gas development. The Government spoke of the benefits that would accrue from the sourcing of materials in Canada and enhancing Canadian producers not only to supply our needs in this field but to develop expertise and eventually sell it offshore. It also included provisions to ensure the procurement of Canadian employment.
The unfortunate fact which became clear when we were discussing this legislation was that it was totally discretionary. The clauses that were written into the legislation were virtually ineffective in providing any teeth, public scrutiny or any input from outside the Minister's office. Although he would have advice from his supporting Departments, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was solely responsible for determining what would happen in this very important industrial sector. I would suggest from the facts that were laid before the committee and the House of Commons when considering the Oil and Gas Act that the Minister's priorities were definitely for developing energy without considering industrial benefits in Canada. Those discretionary powers were far in excess of what was required and certainly excluded many other sectors in the country, including the marine industrial sector, members of organized labour and the public in general who would benefit.
The purpose of this motion is to try to shed some light on these facts. We had envisioned a group of knowledgeable people being convened as an inquiry group which would travel throughout the country to meet with representatives of municipalities, organized labour and the various shipyards and shipbuilders in Canada. They would meet with the oceans industries group who provide materials to the shipbuilding
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
industry so that this inquiry could produce a general and well informed, publicly informed document that could supply some recommendations for improving the marine industrial sector in Canada.
We eventually saw some initiatives on the part of the Government and the acknowledgement that the shipbuilding industry which it had ignored for years was in fact worth the time and investment. I would point out that the federal Government appeared to be interested in developing a shipbuilding policy from what we delivered at the beginning of the year, which advocated a very passive effort with no activity at all.
That passive action came in the form of three basic proposals. It would see the customs boundary extended out 200 miles in the hope of capturing marine activities within Canada, such as marine platforms which would be constructed in Canada in order to escape the duty provisions. This proposal or policy statement, which is all that it is, would eliminate some of the preferential duties that would allow certain nations such as Commonwealth countries and developing nations to dump ships in Canada at much lower prices and without penalties than Canadian shipyards could provide. While obvious loopholes such as that were blocked, that was not the case with the boundary. The boundary was not extended.
Now that the policy is in place I wonder if we will ever see the supporting legislation. It is my understanding that the responsibility now passes from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) to the Secretary of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove). We have no indication that this will occur.
A second token recognition was revealed in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). The Minister of Finance is the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the one who took the position that he would be the end-all and be-all in determining what would happen in Canadian shipbuilding. As Minister of Finance he used his discretion by giving another indication that the Canadian Government had some minor interest in shipbuilding in this country. He indicated that approximately $700 million would be provided for a Coast Guard fleet renovation program.
I would point out, however, that this old plum of the Coast Guard fleet renovation has been trotted out by Cabinet Ministers over the last three Parliaments. Every time that an individual in the Treasury benches requires a plum to trot out during his travelling through the Great Lakes, or on the East or West Coast of the country, he would trot out the old Coast Guard fleet renovation program. When the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) was Minister of Defence in the previous Conservative Government, he proposed a $300 million fleet renovation program. We are still waiting for those vessels.
We also heard about the same fleet renovation program in the previous Parliament. I know that Members of the Party to my right have been asking that the program be put on the drawing board quickly and be accelerated for three purposes. The first is to provide the infrastructure and equipment that the Canadian Coast Guard needs to perform efficiently. The

vessels and floating equipment under construction or on order, with a gross tonnage of 186,000 tonnes. This reflects a reduction of 59 per cent in the number of units under construction and a 35 per cent reduction in tonnage. New orders were down drastically from 38 in 1981 to 11 in 1982. The report goes on to indicate that there are no new orders for 1983 in the order book. This is a desperate situation. With the exception of the soft commitment, the statement of policy on which the Government has not delivered, and the Canadian frigate program, there is very little in the works for the Canadian shipbuilding industry.
In the discussion of the Canada Oil and Gas Act, discussion was had of some of the models other countries such as Norway or Britain develop. I am speaking of the offshore supply office concept. Certain specialists could take a look at Canadian industry where there is potential for development and encourage the taking on of new lines of products that would meet maritime industrial needs, co-ordinating those activities with the shipbuilders, the oil companies and the offshore resource exploration companies who require it.
In Britain they had hundreds and hundreds of people working in the offshore supply office. They were involved in marketing, engineering and in on the ground, hands-on assistance to business in a variety of areas. It was effective assistance. But what did we put forward, Mr. Speaker? We put forward 24 people in the Department of Industry's office of industrial benefits. It is a joke. By the time they get just the simple paper work done and manage to organize it, it is a wonder they can do anything in the area of practical assistance.
Over the next two decades we are looking at the expenditure of billions of dollars. We are talking in the order of $33 billion. There are 400 different projects over the next two decades at which Canadian yards could have a crack. It would employ tens of thousands of Canadians. But the Government in its very soft commitment wants 24 people to do all that work. It is ridiculous. That is a failure to deliver on the commitment.
I say to the Government double or triple the resources. This is not Goverment intervention; it is a desperate and real need to co-ordinate and disseminate information to encourage the private sector to take on more activities. Some assurance should be given in the beginning that the investment will find a return. That can be guaranteed by proper timing of programs and by proper resources allocated to assist business to get rolling in this important field.
It is interesting that over the years on the merchant fleet side we probably have had a very large Canadian-owned merchant fleet, with companies such as Federal Commerce and Navigation, Canadian Pacific and Papachristidis Mara-time Inc. A large number of Canadian firms benefit by registering those ships offshore. They have tax concessions and reduced requirements for employee benefits and benefits like that. This Government could very quickly see those ships returned to Canada. We would have ready made employment for shipyards, ready made business for Canadian crews and the entire secondary area of employment and economic opportunities that accrue out of it. This Government could very quickly
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
put those Canadian ships onshore by one simple method. It could adopt the UNCTAD procedure of cargo reservations and say that the selling of Canadian goods offshore would be applied under the UNCTAD proposal. Then those shipping companies would come onshore to carry our goods. They are carrying them already, but the benefits are going elsewhere.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF APPOINTING ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) for moving his motion today. He almost apologized for doing so and questioned whether or not it was relevant since he placed it on the Order Paper back in November, 1981. I want to assure him that it is very relevant today.
I am pleased that he acknowleged the federal Government is interested in the deep sea fleet subject. Also I was very pleased he gave the federal Government some recognition because we have done something modestly, as he put it. He also gave recognition to the present budget which earmarked over $700 million for the Canadian Coast Guard Fleet Renovation and Acquisition Program.
More important, his motion allows us to present to Canadians what has and what has not been done in this entire area. As the Hon. Member probably knows very well, Canada made a conscious decision in the late 1940s to rely on market forces for international shipping requirements, which led to the demise of the post-war inefficient Canadian flag fleet. This does not mean, however, that the Government has ignored the issue of Canada's participation in ocean shipping over the past 30 years. Several very extensive studies have been commissioned over past years to ascertain whether or not it would be in the Canadian interest to encourage the development of a Canadian presence in deep sea shipping. Before recommending further studies or Royal Commissions, as the Hon. Member suggested, I think it behooves us to examine some of the history and results of earlier studies.
In order to understand better the present situation, it is important to go back to the situation which prevailed after the Second World War. In 1945 the Park Steamship Company was administering a fleet of 176 vessels. By 1948 the Canadian fleet comprised 215 dry-cargo vessels totalling two million deadweight tons. The post-war shortage of shipping services and high ocean freight rates allowed Canadian vessels to operate in the deep sea trades despite the fact that Canadian flag operating costs were the second highest in the world. By the end of the decade, however, growing competition from foreign fleets, a drop in world freight rates, labour problems and changing technology began to tell upon Canada's merchant marine.
After a substantive review of the international shipping situation in 1948-49, the Canadian Marine Commission concluded that:
Having regard to the cost of construction and operation and taking trade balances into consideration, it is inadvisable as well as uneconomic for Canada to

May II, 1983
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
consider the construction and operation of a Canadian flag, ocean-going merchant marine of sufficient dimensions to accommodate all her export trade or any fixed percentage thereof.
The Commission recommended that Canada maintain the shipping and shipbuilding industries as a nucleus capable of rapid expansion in an emergency. The Government, however, conscious of the difficulties faced by the Park fleet, decided to rely fully on market forces and approved a liquidation of the inefficient Park fleet. Owners were given seven years in which to use the proceeds of the sale of war-built ships for the acquisition of new or reconditioned ships, preferably ones built in Canadian shipyards. Because owners were reluctant to build deep sea tonnage, a large portion of the sale proceeds were ultimately diverted into lake and coastal shipping. It is worth noting that these fiscal privileges were a key element in the development of the Canadian Great Lakes fleet, which not only serves as a low-cost, efficient carrier of Canadian domestic cargoes, but has managed as well to capture a large proportion of the marine cargoes moving between the United States and Canada. I am told that this now amounts to about 90 per cent.
Ever since the decision to liquidate the Park Steamship Company, the debate has been going on as to whether or not it is economically sound to revive the Canadian deep sea fleet. Although there has been in the past, and continues to be, selective participation by Canadian flag shipping in specialized deep sea trades, it is generally recognized that Canada may not possess a world-wide comparative advantage in the deep sea shipping sector which would allow the country to become a major maritime power. The conclusions of the various studies have been similar. Although Canadians face some cost disadvantages, the studies all pointed out the potential for Canadian participation in certain trades, particularly those where capital intensive vessels were required.
In 1970, after the passing of the National Transportation Act, a report prepared by Hedlin Menzies and Associates for the Canadian Transport Commission assessed the potential feasibility of a Canadian deep sea merchant marine. The Hedlin Menzies study was an exhaustive evaluation of the economics of deep sea shipping. Construction and operating costs were obtained for both Canadian and foreign flag operators. A computerized economic evaluation model was used to identify prototype ships that would result in minimum carrying costs for each major Canadian deep sea bulk trade.
In total, 26 separate East and West Coast Canadian trade patterns were examined, which embraced various Canadian trade cargoes, possible cross-trades and possible ship types. On the basis of these most efficient ships, the study then calculated the freight rates and revenues operators would require. They concluded that Canadian flag operators would require annual revenues between 14 per cent to 20 per cent higher than those required by low-cost foreign flag owners in order to achieve the same after tax return on equity. They attributed the higher required revenues to the impact of Canadian taxes and the higher operating costs caused by Canadian crew and subsistence costs. Despite this general cost situation, the study identified as potentially economic for Canadian owners those
trades using bulk-type vessels with capital costs in excess of $10 million, using 1975 dollars.
An exhaustive study of the commercial viability of shipping into and out of Canada was carried out in the late 1970s by Alcan Shipping Services Limited. The basic message from the Alcan report with respect to the commercial viability of the various options studied was that a number of routes were potentially profitable for Canadian entrepreneurs. The Alcan study examined the relative competitiveness and profitability of foreign flag shipping versus Canadian flag options and tested them against 23 selected commodity routes accounting for 54 per cent of Canadian 1974 deep sea exports and 30 per cent of deep sea imports in tonnage terms. These included 12 bulk routes, five neo-bulk routes, four container routes and two break-bulk routes. For purposes of analysis, costs and revenues were projected for each route on the assumption that vessels appropriate to the nature and amount of the cargoes involved would be employed.
The 12 bulk commodity routes accounted for 55 per cent of Canadian deep sea bulk exports and 35 per cent of deep sea bulk imports in 1974. The five neo-bulk routes accounted for 48 per cent of all neo-bulk Canadian deep sea trade during the same year, and the four container routes represented 78 per cent of Canada's container trade.
The study did not attempt to select routes for potential Canadian investment. It simply examined the commercial attractiveness of these four options. Results were based on anticipated average conditions over a 20-year period. A typical vessel was identified for each route and traffic flow volumes estimated. Future freight rates were calculated, as well as future vessel costs. Other variables included were vessel purchase and charter costs, payment schedules and loan terms, write-off periods, maintenance and crewing costs, port and fuel costs, market freight rates and appropriate discount rates.
The analysis indicated that Canadian-built and Canadian registered ships could prove profitable on seven routes. Canadian registered ships obtained from the cheapest source of supply were considered potentially profitable on six routes.
In light of these types of findings, it is difficult to find justification for any further studies of the commercial competitiveness of prospective Canadian operators in deepsea shipping. In fact, there are many reasons why it is very difficult to compare Canadian flag operations with foreign operations, a large proportion of which are influenced by various Government assistance programs. First, there is very little economic regulation of the international shipping industry. Hence reliable and timely cost data is very difficult to come by.
Second, the international deepsea industry is a very large industry which is not homogeneous. Conditions which prevail in one part of the industry may not be similar in another. There are a variety of types of operations with often a clear separation in the behaviour of various market segments. For example, there are the three principal shipping markets, liquid bulk, dry bulk and general cargo, as well as the specialty
May 11, 1983

markets such as heavylift, short-sea, roll-on-roll-off-ferries, cruise ships and more. Each one of these is completely different in the type of size of vessels employed, often in the ports they serve and the economic conditions which affect them. Thus, simultaneously it is possible to have a boom in the bulk carrier market due to extraordinary wheat purchases by an East European nation, a bust in the large tanker market due to a crisis in the Persian Gulf, a simultaneous boom in the offshore supply vessel market in the hunt for alternate resources, and a slump in the cruise market due to a recession in the United States. Thus it is not possible to draw conclusions about the industry that are applicable to all situations.
Third, the ocean shipping industry is very volatile with rapid changes in rates and in second-hand ship costs, as these reflect the capitalized value of earnings potential. In very few sectors, is it more evident than in international shipping that forces combine to make it a volatile sector. Transportation being a derived demand, all cycles affecting one particular commodity or specific trade route are immediately passed on to shipping in terms of reduced volumes, rates or irregular patterns. On the other hand, ar demonstrated by the world petroleum pricing situation, the increases in commodity prices are not necessarily reflected by higher freight rates, although often there may be a relation between the value of commodities and the level of rates.
Rates are also affected by political factors such as the closing of the Suez Canal or military activities, creating a demand for commercial shipping, as demonstrated by the Korean and Vietnamese wars. Any analysis of freight rates in the international marine sector will quickly show that rates fluctuate violently, not uncommonly rising by some 250 to 350 per cent within weeks, if not days, then dropping just as rapidly to original levels or even well below.
An illustration of rate fluctuations is transportation charges for wheat between Canadian St. Lawrence River ports and Antwerp, Amsterdam and Rotterdam. Ocean charter freight rates from these St. Lawrence ports on a yearly weighted average basis were $10.84 U.S. per tonne in 1973, rising to $18.18 U.S. in 1980 and falling back to $6.31 per tonne by 1982, a level only 60 per cent of the rates prevailing nine years earlier.
It is very important to note the fact that Canada does not have a major deep sea fleet does not mean that there has been no participation by Canadians in the industry. As of the beginning of 1982, total registered tonnage of the Canadian merchant fleet of 1,000 deadweight tonnes and over under the Canadian flag amounted to $3,600,000 deadweight tonnes and included 271 ships. Of these ships, 85 were identified as being able to navigate on the oceans but only a few were actually engaged in deep sea services, the majority of vessels being used almost exclusively in domestic coasting or transporter trades.
An important fleet, which is indicative of Canadian interest in shipping and illustrates the potential for more direct participation, is the one controlled by Canadians but registered abroad. Although no official Canadian records show the real extent of Canadian control, estimates prepared by the Canadian Transport Commission show that at the end of 1982
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
Canadians controlled at least 108 ships which totalled over 6.5 million deadweight tonnes. Controlled by companies such as Canadian Pacific Limited, Cast North American Limited and Fednav, Limited, this fleet is registered in countries such as the United Kingdom, Liberia, Belgium and Hong Kong.
The largest and one of the most successful components of the Canadian flag fleet is the fleet operating in the inland waters of the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River. Canadian Government support for the Canadian laker fleet was extensive following the opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959. The result of these policies was a Canadian flag fleet that expanded rapidly to take advantage of the larger ship sizes made possible by the new Seaway locks.
As well as moving domestic Canadian trade on the Great Lakes, the Canadian lake fleet moves over 90 per cent of the transborder cargoes between Canada and the United States. The solid establishment of a Canadian fleet on the Great Lakes and similar successes on both coasts in the domestic and transborder trades show that given the proper environment, Canadians can operate successfully and innovate to remain competitive. For example, Canadian ship owners have pioneered the use of self-unloader ships in the Great Lakes, and on the West Coast many tugs or barges have been designed to serve specific needs of the forest industry. As well, those successful operators have demonstrated the feasibility and viability of using Canadian crews and dealing with unions in a constructive and stable manner.
As well as successes in domestic and transborder trades, certain Canadian operators have discovered commercially viable selective opportunities in deep sea trades based on some market or technological advantage. The most recent venture in this direction has been the decisions of some of our Canadian Great Lakes ship owners to build ships that are capable of operating both in the deep sea trades and in the Great Lakes.
Two of these ships were delivered last year, a further five are being delivered this year and a final two are scheduled to be delivered in 1984. At an average cost of $40 million each, these nine ships constitute a very large financial commitment by Canadian ship owners and reflect the belief of Canadian ship owners that they can compete in certain deep sea trades based on the advantage of the self-unloading technology which they have developed in the Great Lakes and based on the strength of their present domestic operations.
However, a study recently completed by Professor Shaw of York University for the Canadian Transport Commission argues that the technological advantage which these ships presently enjoy may be lost in a few years as operators of foreign flag shipping gain access to the same technology. He argues that the tax rules applicable to these Canadian operations will have to be changed if these new ocean-going lakers are to continue to operate in deep sea shipping on a commercial basis.
The Government is continuing to determine the specific tax and shipping policies which will create an environment that will be more attractive for deep sea operators to invest in

May 11, 1983
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
Canada. I have more to say but I see, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time is up.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF APPOINTING ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I compliment the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) on bringing forward this motion to create a royal commission on maritime industrial opportunities within Canada. There is no need for him to apologize about the timing of his motion, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) said.
In my opening comments I want to say how sorry some of us on this side are for the Parliamentary Secretary when he has to stand up in this House and read a memorandum prepared by some bureaucrat deep in the bowels of the marine section of the Department of Transport, feeding out information that they assembled. I believe that memorandum may have been circulated in the form of a magazine or an article directed to the nation at large. It would be nice to hear the Parliamentary Secretary speaking from his gut and from his heart about how he feels as a person representing the people rather than as a bureaucrat deep within the system.
This very, very critical issue is uppermost in the minds of most of us who reside in the Maritime areas and regions of Canada. The mover of the motion, myself and another colleague here in the House come from the West Coast. In my riding alone there are eight shipyards including one major shipyard. These eight shipyards have pioneered the technology that created ships to service the emerging oil industry in the North Sea and the offshore rigs. They have designed and built marvellous vessels that work in the Arctic Ocean and serve the drilling rigs and islands in the Arctic.
We now have an unbelievable technology that has emerged from the marine colleges of the world. I would say that the marine architects from the West Coast stand second to none. Our products can be delivered all over South America, into Asia, Europe and the North Sea. What we on the West Coast seem to want is equal and fair treatment by the Export Development Corporation that will enable us to put together compatible packages that are small enough to allow us to deliver the great fishing technology and service technology and auxiliary vessel technology that has been developed on the West Coast.
I have struggled with the bureaucracy here in Ottawa many times to try to get the Export Development Corporation to recognize the needs of the West Coast consortiums that deal in only a few million dollars, but these few million dollars are very important to this type of highly specialized shipyard. If the package is not in the hundreds of millions of dollars, the Export Development Corporation does not seem to be interested in it. It is too much bother in terms of the red tape and paper work that must be done. That really is a tragedy. We are losing much of our ability to build and service our domestic Maritime needs because of the total financial packages coming from shipbuilding countries that have similar design and architectural capacities but have perhaps a far higher level of productivity with lower cost.
The essential difficulty that the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) is trying to overcome is something that I have pondered and struggled with quite a bit. We in the House keep telling ourselves that it is our national need to improve national productivity at all levels, and that to challenge costs and really bring inflation down to levels where mankind is served properly by the system, productivity must be improved. As we improve our productivity, the capital quotient of production will have to be improved. We will have to improve the person-hours in production as a quotient and we will have to bring capital and labour into optimum balance.
Just recently the Government saw fit to announce that it will finance a productivity centre in order to bring us out of the productivity dilemma that we are faced with in this country. Well, is it not interesting that the Right Hon. Mr. Diefenbaker structured a productivity centre back in the 1960s that the Liberal Government then closed? We have now returned to more rhetoric on the need for productivity.
I believe that the essence of truth in terms of our need for productivity is something that we as politicians in the House who stand for election are failing to grapple with. It is far more important to grab money from the federal pot and sprinkle it around our ridings than face up to some hard facts. I would love to take to my riding some of the Coast Guard fleet renovation programs.
Mr. Speaker, what is being done in the Coast Guard fleet renovation program? As I understand it, the major dollars involved in that program will replace three of the larger Coast Guard vessels that are used as buoy tenders, channel tenders and so on. Just last Monday I was told by a very responsible official in the Department that there were ten to 15 years of life left in each of three vessels that this Coast Guard fleet renovation program will replace. The new vessels will have an efficiency in fuel consumption that is lacking in the old vessels, but the old vessels were very efficient and well constructed with ten to 15 years of good service left in them for the duty that they perform; but here we are phasing them out at a time when they have no market value. They will go to the scrapyard. We will deliver these three new vessels in order to create some temporary work in our shipyards and probably in order to upgrade accommodation on those vessels for the employees of the Coast Guard. It seems to me to be very wasteful and tragic to resort to that kind of program in order to make work.
On the other hand, what if we were to direct our energies back to ALRT, the automatic rail transport system that is being installed in Vancouver for Transpo 86? Why does this Government not take a type of export development credit and put together a financial package on the ALRT, and give this country a domestic working model from the Lower Mainland all the way up through the Fraser Valley on both sides of the river to open up a whole new vista of land and lower the cost of housing and living within the Lower Mainland of British Columbia?

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF APPOINTING ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
We will not sell the Canadian ALRT program until there is a complete working model at home in our own land. ALRT was originally justified because there is something like a $4 billion world market for this type of technology. We in Canada will not be able to sell on the world market. We do not have a really efficient working model on a domestic urban scale because the financial package has not been available to that demonstration project.
What I am getting at is that if we are to resolve the problems we are facing today, we must address the national productivity. In order to address productivity we will have to be honest with ourselves and stop being so political and dishonest with our national interests.
We are now in the age of GATT. A struggle with protectionism is going on in the country. We are trying to break down barriers and open up free trade. Mr. Speaker, we have a very hard five to eight years ahead of us adjusting to international free trade. How are our shipyards and steel industries to compete when Canadian labour is at S20 an hour, Japanese labour is at $9 an hour and Korean labour is at $4 an hour? Right there in the labour quotient of capital goods is a productivity challenge.
These are problems that must be addressed. Maybe the royal commission that our colleague from the NDP is calling for will address those problems. But a royal commission consisting only of shipping interests and Maritime union interests, totally self-interested, would be a total waste of money and a national tragedy. If we are to structure a royal commission, we must open it up to all input from the nation and the world in order to find a solution that is meaningful. It is a basic change in attitude, it is a basic change in work ethic, it is a basic emphasis on the word "productivity" which is needed if we are ever going to move ourselves into the world of a competing Maritime nation.
The essence of having a Maritime fleet is to be able to compete with those countries which attract a Maritime fleet. That means creating a tax system which is compatible with the international world of reality in shipping. You cannot create a Maritime fleet under the tax system and tax law we have in Canada. It is just impossible. The Parliamentary Secretary told us there were 108 Canadian ships on the high seas all sailing under other flags, except for our domestic inland fleet. Therefore we must be realistic with some fundamental truths and stop trying to pump out this dishonest rhetoric and programs like the Coast Guard fleet renovation program, the recycling of $4 billion for reconstruction in the West and the recycling of double-track every six months, in every budget speech or in every Prime Minister's speech. The rhetoric has to stop and some basic honesty has to go into the hard issue of the challenge which is ahead of us in this House in the years ahead.
In addressing this problem, another essential consideration is where are the world's markets for products from Canadian resources and Canadian manufacture? There are none. There
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
are no buyers in the world for what has filled the bottoms of ships.
We do, however, make some moves in the direction of Canadian interests. I can remember back in the Thirty-first Parliament being part of the Government when we insisted that Cominco take 50 per cent of ore from its mines in the North to Europe in a Canadian bottom. They thought we were being very hard on them because we were penalizing them with the higher cost of shipping that tonnage in a Canadian bottom when they could get a lower price from other vessels available to them on the world market. Therefore we were penalizing them for being Canadian, harvesting Canadian minerals and shipping them to foreign markets. There was quite a debate on that issue, but the Minister of Transport of that day hung on. The fact that there are now reduced markets for our products is an indication of the trouble which Canadian National, that great Crown Corporation is in with Cast. Much wiser private sector people want out when they see what is ahead, but the Crown Corporation goes in and invests all kinds of money in Cast and now has some real economic headaches.
When we start to talk about a Maritime industry for Canada, we should go back to some of our recent experiences in the last decade and a half. I refer to the building of these beautiful tugs and supply vessels to North Sea oil drilling rigs and that whole vast capital explosion which took place, which kept the eight shipyards in my riding completely busy putting out these beautiful little ships. These tug companies which built and contracted these ships had them under a Canadian flag could not get Canadians to man them. These ships, between the steel walls, had a rubber lining so there was no vibration and noise inside the ships. I had never been on ships of such comfort and of such a high standard for crews. The wages some ten years ago were $20,000 to man these tugs and you could not find Canadian seamen to man them. The seamen came from Portugal and Spain. Even today when Canadians do go aboard these ships in the North Sea and the Arctic, where do they live? They are flown back and forth to Spain and Portugal. That is part of their contract; three weeks on, three weeks off. When we have that level of anticipation among maritime union members who want us to develop a Maritime fleet, we have to look at the emerging Third World and what other people in the world will work for. If we are not going to be productive and competitive, using our brains to be productive and competitive, then why do we keep talking about a Maritime nation? It does not make economic sense?
I mentioned the example of ALRT where we have a chance of moving out into world markets along with our technology, if we complete the financial package. It has been proven that we must look at these areas instead of pouring all our dollars into losers. I was Minister of State for Industry and Small Business for a short period of time. In our budget of 1979-80 we were pouring something like $78 million into subsidies for shipbuilding. There was no Government program which was more costly in terms of work creation than that program which was

May 11, 1983
Maritime Industrial Opportunities
subsidizing ships built in Canadian shipyards. I believe the total benefit was for about 3,300 workers and we were pumping some $78 million into it. That is why both Governments have had to reconsider this program. It is just not equitable to pump that kind of tax dollars into that industry for the benefit of 3,300 or 3,400 workers. I remember making the very hard decision to send the subsidy down to build the last three Canadian fish trawlers built in Canada in Halifax. The rest since then as the Parliamentary Secretary said, have come in from offshore.
I have always believed that we have the technology and the efficiency to build vessels for the harvesting of our national resources in Canada. But we get all tangled up again in dishonest politics. It was the Liberal Government which denied Northland Navigation on the West Coast the right to spend some $22 million of their own money to put in a ro-ro fleet, to put in docks, so that the whole North Coast of British Columbia could be served with modern transport. The Liberal Government denied it, wiped them out, bankrupted the company and gave $4.2 million a year to the Province of British Columbia, who have had a disastrous situation ever since. There was total disregard for the outback, for the people who still use outhouses, out on the frontiers of Canada.
The Parliamentary Secretary mentioned freight rates. In markets of the world, where there is a balance between supply and demand, freight rates are one of the most critical issues which people involved in marketing and commodities deal with. I have been in the world of freight rates all my life. I lose the City of Winnipeg as a market when freight rates change. I lose the City of Regina when freight rates change. I lose the City of Saskatoon when freight rates change. I cannot move products beyond the eastern boundary of Alberta when freight rates change. Back in the Thirty-first Parliament I remember screaming in this House for weeks at a time over the antidumping decision brought about by Algoma Steel whereby it denied our West Coast steel industry steel from offshore because they had surplus capacity here in Ontario. As soon as it won that case, it changed the freight rates so that finished steel going to the West Coast had the same freight rate as raw steel. Consequently, if it had not been for the dropping of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the United States dollar, all of our steel workers on the West Coast would have been out of work.
That is the kind of lack of equity which we have to address if we are going to bring strength back to this nation and some kind of long-term, meaningful work. It is only in the area of productivity and sensible application of national resources that we are going to have anything which lasts beyond just a little buffer over the next 6 to 18 months.
