subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CANADA DAY AND DOMINION DAY
speechtext:
that Bill C-680, an Act to amend the Holidays Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-680, an Act to amend the Holidays Act, is an important Bill and I have great pleasure in moving second reading. The purpose of the Bill is to emphasize the fact that the constitutional independence of Canada was achieved on April 17, 1982 by the proclamation of the Canada Act, 1982. Consequently, April 17, under this Act, would be celebrated in the future as Canada Day. The naming of July 1, marking the beginning of the Dominion of Canada, as it was known in 1867, would be restored to its historically more appropriate name of Dominion Day.
I want to emphasize today, Mr. Speaker, that we are a young nation and we should be putting great stress and emphasis on our historical beginnings. In many countries in Europe, and in Great Britain, we see how they preserve their history and traditions by marking them; yet in this country we have not realized the importance of commemorating those things which were so important to the beginning of our nation. I want to see July 1 restored as Dominion Day for many historic reasons and I want to outline a few of them, just as I
May 11, 1983

want April 17 to be remembered for historical reasons as Canada Day.
Back in 1867, when Dominion Day came into its own, it was a tremendous challenge to the Fathers of Confederation. When the name Dominion of Canada was chosen it represented a great deal to every Canadian, whatever his origin might be. Dominion Day commemorates a great feat in history as far as Canada is concerned. It signifies the making of a nation, indeed the making of a new nation. It signifies that two peoples of different background, different creeds, different history, language and religion came together and formed a nation.
Even though there were many, many obstacles, discouragements and frustrations, the Fathers of Confederation still went to Charlottetown and together the four Provinces, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec, or Upper and Lower Canada as they were then called, formed a new nation.
It was a huge country, Mr. Speaker, running for hundreds of thousands of square miles with relatively few people. There was practically no industry. Manufactured goods came mostly from Britain and through United States ports. Central Canada knew little about the Maritimes and the Maritimes knew little about Ontario and Quebec. There was no railways as such. The only railway was one which came from and went back to the United States, known as the Grand Trunk. There were poor communications. Yet the Fathers of Confederation had the vision of a great country to be.
So my first reason for wanting July 1 restored as Dominion Day is the fact that it commemorates and honours the Fathers of Confederation for the stand they took and the imagination and vision they showed at that time.
Confederation was also an act of faith; faith that a country could be successful; faith that people could live in the cold climate of Canada, particularly that of the far North; faith that there was a heritage worth preserving; faith that it was a country worth developing; faith that a great nation could be built. Looking back, I think we have again to honour the vision and determination of the Fathers of Confederation in their promise and faith of what this country could do and could be.
My third reason for wanting Dominion Day restored is that it maintains the heritage not of one race but two. The union of the four states at that time, and later all the rest of the Provinces of Canada, was an act between people of two different origins, two different languages, two different creeds, the English and the French. The determination was that each of those people would keep their roots and those roots would be embodied in this great new land, so the Fathers of Confederation sought a name that would show that Anglo-Saxons would keep their roots and the French would keep their roots.
They thought of many names. There were many names suggested and discarded. There was the suggestion that it be called the Kingdom of Canada, but there were objections to that. Then Sir Leonard Tilley produced from the Seventy-second Psalm something that thrilled the people of that day
Holidays Act
and which has thrilled Canadians of all origins ever since. It reads:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, from the river unto the ends of the earth.
Shall have dominion, Mr. Speaker, from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth. The Fathers of Confederation, of both origins, accepted that name and the Queen consented. That is when the Dominion of Canada was born.
This new nation was a small nation, but it had the vision of those Fathers of Confederation that we would some day build a greater and greater nation. Yes, it embodied the desire to bring all of the Provinces into the union. And it did. They were not content to have just New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec as part of the union; they looked across the nation. They looked north and west and east and saw the tremendous possibilities. That vision has become a reality. We now have Provinces all the way to the Pacific Ocean; we have Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland to the east and we have two great potential Provinces, the Northwest Territories and Yukon, to the north.
The Fathers of Confederation embodied that vision again in the name "Dominion of Canada". That tells us something of our history.
This country is founded on a belief in God, on Christianity. We recognize the religions of all peoples and do not say ours is the only religion, but the country was founded on the precepts of the Bible and on the precepts of God. We became a Christian nation. Whoever had the power in the Government of this new nation decreed that that power, provincially or federally, would be exercised under God. Too often today we start to cut the roots that bound us at the beginning; what bound the Provinces together was a firm belief in the omnipotent God. We have to go back to that if we are to reach the potential that the Fathers of Confederation envisioned.
That vision implied that more than two cultures would join to form this new nation. It implied that people from all over the world could come to this vast land and build a new nation. That is all embodied in the words "Dominion of Canadian"- "from sea to sea, from the river unto the ends of the earth".
That is a reality now. People from every country in the world now live in these domains. We live together peacefully for the most part, bound by the objectives and visions of the Fathers of Confederation which were to build a great nation where freedom would be the byword and belief in God would be basic to everything.
Dominion of Canada implies that this nation would not be four separate states but a nation with a federal Government and provincial Governments. There is a division of powers as set out in the British North America Act and it would be federally united into one dominion, with the constitution similar to that of the United Kingdom.
That is part of the history of the early days that we would lose if we threw aside the day that was established as the
25362

May 11, 1983
Holidays Act
birthday of this great country. It implied also parliamentary responsibility and a Government that would be answerable and accountable to the people. It was never intended that it would simply be done by majority Government without consultation and without full and free discussion. The Fathers of Confederation saw this vast country developing through discussion and consensus. It implied the rule of law-that this country would be ruled by law and that the Government would obey the law in the same way as the humblest citizen would be required to do. That is the vision that is tied up in the name of Dominion Day.
It implied also our membership in the great British Commonwealth of nations, and that too is a reality today. Two or three weeks ago I had the pleasure of attending a ceremony in Westminster Abbey where representatives of 18 Commonwealth countries, men and women of all colours, creeds, religions and language, met united as part of the British Commonwealth. Each had his flag, his language, his differences, his own form of democratic government, but all were there as members of the Commonwealth of Nations. When the Fathers of Confederation made Canada a nation instead of four separate states, they brought us into that great commonwealth of nations.
I was thrilled when I saw Her Majesty the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh walk through that throng of people in Westminster Abbey. Representatives of 18 countries, including Canada, carried their flags proudly and put them on stands on the platform during that service.
We need to honour tradition in this country by remembering how the Dominion of Canada was formed and why it was formed. Our friends in Quebec say, "Je me souviens". It appears on their license plates and it means "I remember". Let us remember the history of this country and give every citizen, irrespective of language and country of origin, the chance to remember the beginning of this nation called Canada, this nation of which we are proud to be a part.
We have to show vision as the Fathers of Confederation did when they started out with the four states. Now we have this vast part of the continent as the Canadian nation.
On April 17 last year the Canada Act was proclaimed and Canada severed its dependence on Britain but not its membership in the Commonwealth of Nations. Canada became independent. Now we do not have to approach the British Parliament for approval or the British High Court to finalize our court cases.
The Bill was signed on April 17, 1982. It shows a tremendous interest in the future. It shows vision. We are to continue to be members of the Commonwealth, and our links with the monarchy of which we are all so proud will continue. Our Queen is the Queen of Canada. April 17 has a great significance as it marks an important moment in the history of Canada.
I ask all Members of the House and the people of Canada to remember our past, to build for the future. Let us remember it by restoring Dominion Day to our laws and by ensuring that
we expect April 17, Canada Day, to have meaning for the future.
We can serve the people of this country well by restoring to this nation Dominion Day as the birth of the Dominion of Canada and Canada Day when the Canada Act was passed.
Mr. Maurice Bossy (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to say a few words concerning Bill C-680. As Hon. Members know, last year on July 1, Dominion Day was changed to Canada Day. The change in the title reflected several needs in Canadian society; the need for a modern application to reflect modern Canada and a name which reflected the identity of the country rather than denoting a status.
The name of this country is Canada; Canada is a name that is known throughout the world. The word "Dominion", while a perfectly good English word, presents difficulties for some people.
Like so much in society, language evolves. The word "Dominion" appears, in some ways, to be old-fashioned or even archaic. It also translates very poorly into French. "Puissance" appears to be the nearest one can come to it in French. Canada is the same in English or French.
What better name for our national holiday than the name of the country itself, a name of which all Canadians can be proud.
It is suggested in Bill C-680 that April 17 should be Canada Day to emphasize that the constitutional independence of Canada was achieved on April 17, 1982. I wonder if the Hon. Member has considered how confusing this change would be to most Canadians, many of whom have been informally referring to July 1 as Canada Day for years, even before its official designation.
I believe that Canadians do not want to become confused by juggling names, titles and dates. There already is a Canada Day. It is July 1, and it honours the Canadian Constitution. The celebrations take note of what happened on July 1, 1867. They also take note of what happened on April 17, 1982. Canada Day is a day on which to celebrate Canada's nationhood. We do not need to have separate days to celebrate separate significant dates in our nationhood. It can all be celebrated together on one day, Canada Day on July 1.
Many polls have been taken to assess how Canadians see the terms Canada Day and Dominion Day. In fact, data tabled before the Senate committee last year said conclusively that Canadians of all cultural persuasions preferred the title Canada Day. Public opinion was measured last year by the National Committee for Canada's Birthday. It suggested that, on the average, the title Canada Day is three times more popular than Dominion Day. Why should we go against public opinion by taking up the name Dominion Day once more?
I wonder if Bill C-680 is primarily concerned with ensuring that the events of April 17, 1982 are well commemorated, or whether the Bill is simply a backdoor attempt to get back to
May 11, 1983

the term Dominion Day. Many Hon. Members took the change in the title as an insult and as a way of denigrating Canada's past. That attitude does not reflect the truth of the situation.
The Montreal Gazette dealt with the word Dominion in an editorial on March 10, 1981. I will quote that editorial which reflects well the difference between Canada Day and Dominion Day. It states:
The word 'Dominion' does have a secure and honored place in Canada's history. But not all historical labels remain accurate; this one certainly has not.
At the time of Confederation the word 'Dominion' was hit upon as a new coinage to describe a country which was not, in fact, a sovereign state (as Canada was not in 1867).
But for the past 50 years Canada has been, in all but a narrow constitutional technicality (which should also be rectified this year), a truly independent nation.
It should not retain a label which was coined to describe a colonial link.
Furthermore, 'Dominion' is not nearly as felicitous a word in French as in English. For French-speaking Canadians it is a verbal oddity which serves mainly to inflame old colonial wounds.
It is time to retire 'Dominion Day' gracefully in favor of a name of July 1 which surely no one can find objectionable, 'Canada Day'.
The editorial still rings true today. Surely what we should be doing is trying to build among Canadians a good understanding of the Canadian Constitution and a good understanding of the events both in 1867 and 1982. We do not need two days to do that. One day will suffice, a day known as Canada Day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always exercise great parliamentary caution and I will do so today, as is my normal practice.
I would like to study the issue itself. I believe that the reason for the change in the first place was mainly that people did not understand the history of the word "Dominion". I do not agree with all of what the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said with regard to the implications to be drawn from the term Dominion of Canada. However, I still think there are many people in this country who misinterpreted what Dominion was intended to mean. Many saw that as a reflection or an attempt to continue to tie us back to colonial times. Of course, that was an interpretation that was quite incorrect and an interpretation which did a disservice to the phrase "Dominion of Canada".
As the Hon. Member for Bow River said, the name Dominion came from an entirely different source. It had nothing at all to do with Britain, with the United Kingdom, or the Commonwealth. It had to do with the choice made in Canada by Canadians of an appropriate way to describe Canada. That is what it was. It was an appropriate way to describe Canada. As I recall, the name was chosen in the same way as Australia chose its name when it called itself the Commonwealth of Australia. Consideration was given as to whether to call it the kingdom, the commonwealth or something else. Those names were discarded for the very reasons that people in Canada recognized the duality of our country and, recognizing the facts of the time, they did not want to have a name which reflected a tie simply with Great Britain. They chose Dominion simply because it had a more neutral interpretation, if you will, but also, in a biblical sense, it did reflect the reality of Canada. It was a most appropriate name. Looking back I cannot help feeling that because the teaching of history in the country perhaps was insufficient and inadequate-

-there was allowed to develop a sense that to call a national holiday-the national holiday, I might say, which reflects our allegiance to the country, our pride and commitment to Canada's future-to call it Dominion Day somehow was interpreted to mean that we were discarding the partnership between French and English Canada, that we were

Holidays Act
thrusting upon French Canada a name that reflected association with Great Britain. I do not think that was true at all.

As my colleague says, Cartier agreed to the name, recognizing that it was the name chosen from among many names truly representing what the great land mass of Canada was all about.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CANADA DAY AND DOMINION DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING CANADA DAY AND DOMINION DAY
speechtext:
If it is true that Dominion is old fashioned, is it any more old fashioned than the word "liberal"? I put that to you. Because the word was old and it stemmed from that period in history when the country came together, it seemed to me to be an appropriate word to use to describe a national holiday. I might have gone as far as to change the name of the holiday to the Dominion of Canada Day so there would be no doubt in anyone's mind what we were talking about. Then I think we would have covered all the bases. I think that might have responded more adequately to the sense that a lot of people in the country had. I might just simply have left it alone for the time being because I do not think the change was necessary.
There was a great push on in my causus, particularly from Members representing British Columbia from where my good colleague, the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) comes, that because his birthday happens to be on July 1, we should call it Skelly Day. We decided not to do that. We decided not to promote that in recognition that maybe it did not have sufficient historical value.
The one argument that worries me, if you will forgive me the argument, is the one made about the close ties with the Commonwealth and how Dominion represents that. There is no one more interested in close ties with the Commonwealth than I am, with the possible exception maybe of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). The very reason why the name Dominion came into disfavour was that interpretation. The very reason why it lost the support of one part of the country was that the interpretation did reflect something to do with the Commonwealth, something to do with our very close association with Great Britain, the Queen, and all of the things that go with that.
I am a royalist, a monarchist. I truly believe that we should have a closer association with the Commonwealth. I think it would be in our best interests economically and socially to do that as a country. I think those things are true, but I do not think they should be done at the expense of other things. I do not think they should be done in a way that is overt or in a way that is destructive of the values of our own country, or in any way that would divide our country. I am concerned for the
very reasons put forward by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). He did so in all good faith, I am sure, as he presented his argument, and his argument rested in part on those close associations, which were good and valuable and remain good and valuable but the very reasons used by the Opposition, if you will, to maintain the name of Dominion Day could be used as justification for changing it.
I argued during that period that there was no justification for a change in name, that people misinterpreted Dominion as a word, misinterpreted what it meant, misinterpreted and misunderstood the origins of it. These were not sufficient reasons for the change that was being proposed. What we should have been doing, instead of allowing the change to take place as a result of that misinterpretation, was to make the effort to try to bring to the public's attention what the word Dominion within the phrase Dominion of Canada actually meant. I think we probably failed in that regard. We got caught up in the politics of it. We got caught up in an ongoing argument. I remember it well and I do not want to reflect on it, however, I do remember it well.
There were attempts being made on a daily basis to find time to pass the Government's Bill. As those attempts were being made and, as the House Leader for this Party, I was in the position of having to sit and look for a period of time when the Government would bring forward its own proposal. That time was simply not forthcoming; there did not seem to be enough time. But I remember the arguments that were made during that period. I do think we failed by not persuading the House of Commons to draw away from the issue and take a much broader look at what the word Dominion in the term Dominion of Canada truly means. I do not think, quite truthfully, it makes much difference to Canadians in the over-all what you call the day, as long as it is a holiday. I think that is probably true. An interesting thing happened. Because the Bill was passed in an imperfect form, it got to the Senate, if you remember, and the appropriate wording was not contained within that piece of legislation which changed the Holidays Act. Therefore, we ended up with Dominion Day having been replaced with Canada Day but Canada Day not appearing as a holiday anywhere. That showed the haste with which the matter was dealt and the inappropriate consideration given to it.

To the best of my knowledge and recollection it is entirely possible come that fine day in July we may well find ourselves with Canada Day not being a statutory public holiday. That reflects badly on those of us who pushed it through, if not on those who were not here to oppose it and demand that changes be made.
There is a need to look at the value of history. A couple of weeks ago we had a debate in the House concerning the
May 11, 1983

tourism industry, at which time I pointed out that if one travelled through parts of the United States, one would find plaques and directions to historical monuments. A great sense of American history is clearly evident on the surface of their lives. One could find it everywhere one looks. They hold with some great passion to names that were established many years ago which may no longer reflect the reality of today but in fact reflect the reality of that day. We must be cautious that we are not inadvertently drawn into doing a disservice to our history. On the day the Constitution of Canada was proclaimed by Her Majesty the Queen in front of the Parliament buildings, I am sure Mr. Speaker will recall the downpour of rain. I wore a brand new suit and 1 was soaking wet as I sat there. But that was not the birth of Canada, that was not a new day or a new dawning. Canada was born long before that day. We cannot suddenly begin the process of changing everything that was established some 100-odd years ago simply because we finally achieved the degree of self-Government we felt we ought to have.
It reminds me of a great urban renewal program which was under-way years ago. In those days urban renewal was seen as tearing down everything in the core of cities and building up brand new buildings. Over time it was recognized that in doing that we lost a lot of our heritage and what had been valuable. We lost a lot of history, and people began to look at the situation and say, "Perhaps we should not have done it that way". I draw this to the attention of the House because this may well be what we are doing now. People have come to realize that urban renewal is a process of improvement and also a process of re-establishing what was of significant value to us throughout the years. It is also a process of ensuring that it is kept in a form which makes it useful and makes us proud of it. This could equally be said of the name of our country. No one goes around saying that this is the Dominion of Canada, but that is what it is. To have taken the step we took for the reasons it was taken, which I think are more important than the fact that the step itself was taken-

I am not averse to having another holiday, I must confess, and I am sure many of my colleagues and most of my constituents would love another day off with pay, which is not likely I might add. However, we could achieve the goals we have set for ourselves, recognizing the value of what took place many years ago, and recognizing perhaps the reality of the difficulties that were allowed to develop between French and English-speaking Canada and the misinterpretation that was allowed to pervade the minds of people from coast to coast over the name, if we were to say simply that Canada's national holiday should be the Dominion of Canada Day. Then we would have achieved everything that would satisfy me and probably most other
Holidays Act
people. It would enshrine for all times the purpose and meaning of "Dominion". It would make clear that the choice of the word was made here. It was made originally by Canadians on behalf of Canadians, reflecting Canadian reality, and it would be reaffirmed by Canadians on behalf of Canadians, again reaffirming and reflecting Canadian reality. I hope the House might consider this some day. We would stop the misinterpretation of the word itself and begin to apply it in a positive manner. We would ensure that in a historical sense it was clearly understood that when the Fathers of Confederation decided on that particular wording they did so because they thought it was truly Canadian and nothing else. In that way it reflected the realities and duality of Canada at the time. Now it could perhaps reflect the multinational characteristic of Canada and therefore would be a holiday we could all celebrate together within the sense of "Dominion". If we do that, we might in fact take a step forward rather than subscribe to what I really believe was a step backward taken some time ago.

We owe a debt of gratitude to the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for the Bill he has brought forward today. It is a Bill of reconciliation. We had 12 Orwellians here who tried to rewrite history, and did rewrite history in a way. They could not rewrite the provisions of the Bill to which the present Bill now called the Canada Act referred.
I would refer to the opening of the preamble of that Bill, which was originally known as the BNA Act, enacted by the British Parliament on March 29, 1867. It expressed the desire of the Provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to be federally united into one Dominion under the Crown of Canada. That is in the preamble. A couple of paragraphs
further down it states, "Not only that the Constitution of the legislative authority in the Dominion be provided for". In Article 3 we find that same word. It states that in the Provinces of Canada it shall be lawful for the Queen, et cetera, "Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall form and be one Dominion under the name of Canada" and that on and after that day those three Provinces shall form and be one Dominion under that name accordingly.
I do not quite see how the 12 Orwellian apostles managed on that particular day to change what is there. However, they did try a thing called "you speak or can speak" to produce another name for a day which stands, and I am delighted-oh, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) is gone. He made a worthy contribution to this debate. I am delighted that he did so. I was a little bit concerned by the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Bossy) who wondered whether this was a back door attempt to undo what this Parliament did so much against the rules one day in July, 1982.
I feel we owe a debt of gratitude to the Hon. Member for Bow River for having brought forward this motion. We have not yet decided what we are going to do with April 17. That was a day of importance for Canada. There is no question about that. No matter how you feel about the manner in which the Constitution was produced in Canada and so on, April 17, 1982 was an important day.
On April 17 this year there were a few people who remembered, but it was not a remarkable day in the true sense of the word. It was not marked as a day of importance in our history. It should be. The solution has been provided in this Bill. It should be called Canada Day, and the original day, called Dominion Day to honour the terminology that exists in the Act which created this Dominion, should remain attached to July 1.
It is a wonderful compromise. We can have the best of both worlds, if you like. We do have something to call April the seventeenth day. I know that in Latin America they have a day called Mayo Primero. They have dates attached to celebrations. I think the actual function of that day should be market by a special name. Canada Day is a most suitable name for the designation of April 17. As I say, we went past the first anniversary without really noting it at all.
When that date occurs during a parliamentary session, we might devote it to a discussion of matters relating to Canada. We could have it as an open day. It would be Canada Day and we could celebrate it as such. It need not necessarily be a holiday. It is a day when we could remember the things for which we should be grateful. There are a number of things for which we should be grateful. There are a number of things for which I demonstrate not too much gratitude, but there are a number of things for which I am grateful, and that is one of them.
The Hon. Member for Bow River is not only to be congratulated and commended, but to be thanked for having

brought forward this Bill on this occasion to provide a means of recognizing what happened on July 1, 1967 and on every July 1 there after and also what happened on April 17, 1982. It is a day that should have some sort of recognition.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to thank the Members of the House for their indulgence.
I am pleased to rise today to speak in support of Bill C-676, an Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act. In order to explain briefly the purpose of the Bill, I will run through the major sections of it. The over-all purpose of the Bill is to implement the recommendations of the Canadian Human Rights Commission to add sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination at the federal Government level. As I have noted in the explanatory notes, at the present time homosexuals and lesbians receive no legislative protection whatsoever from discrimination under federal jurisdiction.
The Bill would accomplish two or three objectives. First, it would include in the Canadian Human Rights Act sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination. Second, there is a provision in the Bill which would require the Canadian Human Rights Commission to conduct a comprehensive study of all federal legislation and regulations to determine which, if any, discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation and report the results of this study to the Minister of Justice within one year of the coming into force of the Bill. Following that report, the Minister of Justice would be required to reply to the Commission's report within 60 days outlining proposed action to remove discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation from existing legislation.
I would note one other provision, Mr. Speaker, because there has been some confusion about this provision. Clause 4 of the Bill states explicitly that it is not a discriminatory practice for a person or organization to adopt programs which may be designed to remedy historical discrimination. I would emphasize that in no way does this mandate any form of affirmative action. What it does state, however, is that if an organization or individual had provisions within their hiring practices or otherwise to overcome past inequities, these would not be struck down as being discriminatory.
I would note, and I would particularly draw to the attention of the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), that this

May 11, 1983
Canadian Human Rights Act
provision is identical to the provisions of the Private Members' Bill which was introduced by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), Bill C-242, and which was debated in the House on June 19, 1981. At that time I commended the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre for her introduction of this Bill, and I was certainly pleased to be able to speak in support of the Bill at that time. As I say, the provision in Clause 4 of my Bill today is in fact identical to the provision in Clause 4 of the Private Members' Bill introduced in June by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre.
I have indicated that the primary objective of the Bill is to ensure that the prohibited ground of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is included in the federal Canadian Human Rights Act. This would ensure that there would be no further discrimination at the federal level-and I emphasize at the federal level-in the provision of goods and services or facilities, in access to accommodation or housing, and in employment.
As I emphasized earlier, the purpose of the Bill and the reason I bring the Bill forward today is to ensure that indeed this subject is adequately canvassed by the Justice Committee. I was very pleased that in January of this year, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) gave a commitment to allow the subject matter of this Bill to be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in order that that Committee might hold public hearings and invite public input from a wide variety of groups and individuals to assess the ramifications of this particular amendment. That commitment has been confirmed today by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and I am confident and pleased that that side of the House will indeed live up to the promise made by the Minister of Justice earlier this year. I have also received the assurance of the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre that she will support the Bill. I am confident that she will be speaking on the Bill.
I do want to indicate, Mr. Speaker, that it is very important to note that in Private Members' Hour, the subject matter of a Bill can only go forward as long as it is not talked out by any Member of the House. I have the commitment of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and of the Minister of Justice that that side of the House will not talk out the Bill as indeed was done to the Bill of the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre. Certainly no one in the New Democratic Party will talk out the Bill, and therefore we will be watching the Official Opposition with great interest. I trust that no Member of the Official Opposition will in fact deny the public the right to have input, because all that is being sought at this time is a referral of the subject matter to a committee of the House of Commons where representations may be made. We will be watching with great interest to determine whether or not in fact the Conservative Party is prepared to allow the subject matter of the Bill to go to committee or whether it will block the Bill and deny this important question the kind of discussions that should take place in the Justice Committee.
I would note that there is a wide variety of groups supporting this Bill from a cross-section of Canadian society, including the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Student Christian Movement, of course the New Democratic Party itself at federal and provincial levels, the Anglican Church of Canada, the Mennonite Church of Canada, the United Church of Canada, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Labour Congress, a number of provincial human righs commissions and, as well, the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
In 1979, the Canadian Human Rights Commission recommended for the first time the inclusion of sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in the Canadian Human Rights Act. Every year since that time they have repeated that recommendation. For example, Mr. Speaker, in their most recent report tabled in the House of Commons just a few weeks ago, the Canadian Human Rights Commission states:
The Commission recommends that sexual orientation and political belief be added to the proscribed grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act.
The rationale behind this recommendation was discussed originally in the Commission's 1979 report. The Commission continues to believe that protection is warranted against unfair treatment on these grounds. The Commission's intention is not to see special treatment on these grounds but it does advocate recourse if people are arbitrarily denied opportunities because of prejudice or bias.
I emphasize the point made by the Commission, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill does not in any way seek any kind of special status for homosexuals and lesbians. What it does seek to ensure is that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation must not continue at the federal level.
The recommendations of the Canadian Human Rights Commission followed an extensive study by that Commission. That study in fact was undertaken in response to a letter written by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1978 at the time of the passage of the initial Canadian Human Rights Act. At that time, it was urged by a number of bodies, including those that I have mentioned, that sexual orientation should be included in the Canadian Human Rights Act. However, the Prime Minister stated in a letter of February 4, 1978:
Since the implications of the proposal in Canada have not been fully explored, Canada should not take steps to include it in federal legislation without further comprehensive examination of the problems that might be involved. It is for these reasons that the Minister of Justice has proposed that the question be examined by the Canadian Human Rights Commission which could then make recommendations for further government action.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what happened. And each year for the last five years following that study, the Canadian Human Rights Commission has indeed made recommendations that sexual orientation should be included as a prohibited ground of discrimination.
For five years, the Government, which indicated it wished to hear the views of the Commission, has ignored that important recommendation, a recommendation which may affect some two million Canadians. That is the figure which the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre referred to in her comments in the House in June, 1981. I would note for the record that as a member of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of
May 11, 1983

Canada, I proposed that the prohibited grund of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation should have been included in the equality rights section of the Constitution itself, to apply at all levels of Government, be it federal, provincial or municipal. That amendment, however, was defeated on a vote of 22 to 2 with both the Government and Official Opposition unanimous in their opposition to it.
It is possible that the provisions of the Charter of Rights may in fact be interpreted in such a way that indeed sexual orientation will be a prohibited ground of discrimination. Certainly, that would be my hope. As was indicated by a very distinguished jurist in this country, Mr. Justice Berger, in his book "Fragile Freedoms", "Judges may not always be wiser than politicians but they should be able to stand more firmly against angry winds blowing in the streets." It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that we sought the inclusion of this particular provision in the Charter of Rights itself, to protect this very large minority. As I have indicated, the over-all objective is to ensure an end to discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. It is to ensure that no one can be fired from a job or not hired in a particular area of employment on the basis of sexual orientation. It is to ensure that no one can be thrown out of his or her home on the basis of sexual orientation. It is to ensure access to goods and services which are available to other Canadians.
I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the Bill does not in any way seek any special or preferential treatment whatsoever. It seeks equality. In the Province of Quebec, in December, 1976, such an amendment was passed unanimously by that Legislative Assembly. Fortunately, in the Province of Quebec such protection does now exist for that particular minority.
The Bill also, as I indicated, calls for a full review and response by the Minister of Justice of all legislation and regulations at the federal level. For example, there are a number of provisions of the Criminal Code which certainly are in need of review. Recently, despite the fact that a number of proposals were made by the federal Government in the area of the Criminal Code, the Government caved in, I suppose, to the Canadian equivalent of the moral majority, and refused to make any changes whatsoever to some of the most archaic and repressive provisions of the Criminal Code, whether it was repeal of the offence of gross indecency and the establishment of a uniform age of consent, or the repeal of the bawdy house legislation. We in this House know that in February, 1981 this legislation resulted in the largest mass arrests in the history of this country since the War Measures Act, tactics described by The Globe and Mail as "bully-boy" tactics. I would suggest that police resources are far better deployed in other areas than enforcement of these archaic and discriminatory laws. For example, in the area of violence within the family, wife battering, the police seem most reluctant to get involved, which results in real violence and real harm. Yet they are prepared to spend very significant amounts of time in other areas.
One other provision of the Criminal Code which I believe should be examined is with respect to hate propaganda. I would suggest that the provisions of the Code respecting hate
Canadian Human Rights Act
propaganda should be expanded to include sexual orientation. One need not look far back in our history to see instances of very severe discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. In the Second World War, for example, there was the infamous provision by which thousands and thousands of homosexuals and lesbians were branded with a pink triangle and killed in Nazi concentration camps. This was, of course, very eloquently and graphically documented in a play which I hope all Members of the House would have seen.
Hate literature, whether the object of that hate be homosexuals or other minorities, is the thin edge of the wedge. We have seen recently, for example, in the Province of Alberta, the ugly face of anti-Semitism spreading against the Jewish community. I believe we must make it very clear that hate propaganda, whether on the basis of religion or sexual orientation, is fundamentally unacceptable in a free and democratic society.
There still exist a number of examples, some of them fairly glaring, of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. At the federal level, some of the worst institutional homophobia in Canada exists within the Canadian Armed Forces. For example, the Armed Forces' standing orders require that any suspected homosexual or lesbian be fired from his or her job, no matter how qualified or how capable they may be. And the orders go beyond that and require that all members of the forces must report any suspicious activity. One cannot imagine in Canada in this day and age the prospect of a young man or woman waking up to find two military policemen in their room who would interrogate them for hours, possibly taking them to a cell and threatening them, all on the basis of their suspected sexual orientation. Too many young people have lost their jobs, young people who wanted to serve their country in the Armed Forces and who had outstanding records, and there are hundreds of others who, while they may not have lost their jobs, live in daily fear of being revealed and fired from their jobs without any recourse. I emphasize as well that we are talking about all levels of the Armed Forces.
Hon. Members will know that I raised a number of examples in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. One example was of a young, courageous woman whose name was Zoe Matheson. She told the story of how she was interrogated and threatened on the basis of suspicion and allegations which she was not even given an opportunity to confront. Since I raised that matter publicly, I have received letters from quite a number of other people. I received a phone call from a young man, for example, who had broken down in tears because he was interrogated by the police who went line by line through the letters which he had in his room. It was suggested that he was no longer fit to serve his country.
One cannot imagine that kind of conduct in this day and age. I know that many military people disagree with this policy and in fact, Mr. Speaker, if the amendment which I proposed is adopted, then army officers will be able to come before the Canadian Human Rights Commission and if they can argue successfully that there is a bona fide occupational requirement,

May 11, 1983
Canadian Human Rights Act
let them make that argument. However, these kinds of scare tactics and this kind of blatant institutional homophobia is utterly unacceptable in Canada in this day and age. We must not destroy the careers and perpetrate the kind of fear which is created by this policy at the present time.
The Armed Forces are not alone in this. I need not remind Hon. Members of the fact that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police opened up some 1.3 million files on 800,000 Canadians, many of which have not yet been destroyed. The policies of External Affairs leave much to be desired, and there are many others as well. These are the areas which must be examined, Mr. Speaker, and this is the kind of subject which I would hope would be discussed by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I stated my views very clearly on the occasion of the speech of the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre, that what we are talking about here is a fundamental question of human rights, of the right to live and the right to love without fear of persecution, without fear of discrimination and without fear of the loss of one's livelihood, or one's home, or without fear of being denied goods or services. We are talking about the right of young people in Canada not to be afraid, not to have to keep silent and not to have to conceal their own identity. In fact, we are talking about a fundamental question of the civil liberties of hundreds of thousands of Canadian men and women.
I welcome the agreement of the Minister of Justice to have this subject discussed and considered in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, to give the opportunity to Canadian organizations and individuals to come forward and be heard, whatever their views may be. I would certainly hope, Mr. Speaker, that all Hon. Members of the Official Opposition in the House today would not attempt to subvert this and would not prevent a full hearing being given to this Bill so that all views may be aired. I look forward to their support, Mr. Speaker, and certainly hope that this important question might be studied in the near future by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to say how pleased I am to have the opportunity to speak on this Bill and to support the motion of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), that the subject matter of this Bill go to committee. The reason I do so is that the Bill is very similar to my own Private Member's Bill on this subject, which I put forward two years ago on behalf of my constituents, in particular, and on behalf of the homosexual community in this country.
My own record on this subject is well known. Shortly after my election in 1980 I sponsored Bill C-242 which sought to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation. The Bill grew out of the efforts of the Human Rights Advisory Council in Vancouver, which I had formed at the request of the Hon. Member for Yellow head (Mr. Clark) when he was Prime Minister. The Council was composed of representatives of the
homosexual community who agreed to help me formulate a policy position on the issue of homosexual rights. Our aim then was to draft a Bill which would be referred to committee for study. We wanted to give the homosexual community an opportunity to describe the frustrations, the experiences and hurts unique to their community.
At that time I received a great deal of support from Members of my own caucus, such as the Hon. Joe Clark, the Hon. Flora MacDonald, the Hon. David Crombie and the Hon. Jim McGrath.

I received support from Members of my caucus, such as the Hon. Member for Yellowhead, the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald), the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). However, when the Bill was called for second reading in June, 1981 it was talked out by the Liberals, who were determined to block its study by the Committee. I want to point out that it was not Members of the Conservative Party who talked out that Bill; it was Members of the Liberal Party who talked out a Bill almost identical to the one being presented here today.
I am afraid that the Government is playing that sort of game with this Bill. If the Liberals had really wanted to support the subject matter of this Bill, they had ample opportunity since they killed my own initiative to demonstrate their commitment to the issue. They could have referred my Bill to committee. If they had done so, we would not have to repeat this debate today. Or they could have brought forward legislation of their own. They have had a lot of opportunity to do so in terms of amendments to the human rights legislation. Instead, they are playing a charade today.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) publicly said he will agree to let the subject matter go to committee, but he knows full well that his own caucus does not support it, and he has privately told me that if it does go to committee, his own Party will not support it. So he is taking this public stance in the hope and expectation that Members of my own Party will talk the Bill out. He is hoping that years of Government inaction can be forgotten in the light of one hour's debate this afternoon.
I must say that I also find the NDP hypocritical to be cooperating with the Government in this charade. I think it is hypocritical of the Hon. Member for Burnaby to advance this Bill-and I share his concern-when he knows the Liberals oppose it. He has put us in a situation where the Liberals are making agreements with what the Hon. Member for St. John's East calls the little red rump, the NDP, on an issue when they refuse to allow the Conservative Party to proceed with it. Of course, the NDP can ignore reality because it knows it will never be in Government and will never have to account for its actions. Well, I am more interested in the people than the
May 11, 1983

politics of this issue. I stand on my own record and will continue to work to see that discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation is indeed prohibited.
I will keep my remarks short today but I would like briefly to review my position which I stated nearly two years ago in the House. At that time I pointed out-and this point has been made by the Hon. Member for Burnaby-that I was not asking for a special favour for homosexual Canadians. That is why I do not like the term "gay rights". I have never used that term. What we are talking about is human rights, or what the Canadian Human Rights Commission, headed by a former Conservative MP, Gordon Fairweather, calls unfair treatment. We are not dealing here with additional rights for people. 1 have never advocated and would never advocate special rights for any group in our society, whether men, women or whatever. We are dealing with the issue of equal treatment for human beings on any grounds, whether race, religion, sex or sexual orientation. We are not talking about bestowing privileged status on part of the population. We are talking about extending the same rights to them as other Canadians enjoy and take for granted today.
I think that homosexuals should be able to seek a job, housing, and public services without living in the fundamental fear that they are going to be in some way exposed or made public and deprived of basic human rights. Fundamentally, what homosexuals are asking for is protection, tolerance and the human rights that other Canadians enjoy. My constituents are certainly not asking for extra rights in any way.
Canada is an extremely diverse nation, and for its citizens to live with dignity that diversity must be respected and protected. I believe that most Canadians are, as I was before I became a candidate for election in Vancouver Centre, unaware of the extent of discrimination directed at homosexuals in our society. Most Canadians probably shared my rather benign attitude which combined a lack of interest in the subject with a mild sympathy for people who are not heterosexual. Before I had the opportunity to meet and talk with the homosexual community in my riding I had no idea of the kind of discrimination they face, some of which is overt and obvious and some of which is subtle and hard to prove.
Two years ago, Mr. Speaker, I cited examples of these various kinds of discrimination. We have heard examples today. I told the House about a young man of my acquaintance who was forced to quit a very good job because he lived in fear of discovery as a homosexual. Every day he went to work fearing that his sexual orientation might cost him his job. The fear and tension built up until he decided that he could not live that way any more and he quit. No Canadian should have to endure that kind of suspense and insecurity. I also described cases of harassment by the Armed Forces and by immigration officials simply because people were suspected of being homosexual. We have had examples of that again today. Without being given an opportunity to examine the evidence or to find out where the complaint came from, they were taken to hotels and interrogated in a state close to terror. Nothing was ever proved and nothing needed to be proved. In the interest of time
Canadian Human Rights Act
I will simply state my objective, which is to work to ensure freedom from discrimination for all Canadians.
It is instructive to review developments in the two years since my Bill was talked out by the Liberals. Quebec remains the only Province to have passed human rights protection for homosexuals. Of Canadian cities, Toronto, Ottawa, Windsor and Kitchener have passed human rights measures within their jurisdiction that provide a modicum of protection for homosexuals. Notably, in 1982 Vancouver City Council adopted unanimously in principle what has been termed the most powerful human rights legislation in Canada, and that included among its proscribed grounds of discrimination that of sexual orientation. This legislation remains in limbo at the present time while the city seeks appropriate amendments to the city charter that will allow it to enforce this bylaw.
Human rights protection for homosexuals continues to be supported by Canadian federal and provincial Human Rights Commission. As well as the federal Commission, and Quebec which has enacted legislation, Commissions in B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario recommend inclusion of sexual orientation in their respective provincial codes. Recently the B.C. Commission under Dr. Charles Paris reiterated its recommendation of 1981, and in the last few months the Manitoba Commission has added its support. This means that Human Rights Commission from Quebec to B.C., as well as the Canadian body, now support the concept of Human Rights protection for homosexuals. Unfortunately, human rights infractions continue.
Because sexual orientation is not a ground against discrimination in most Provinces, few accurate tallies of human rights violations against homosexual people have been collected in Canada. However, since 1977 and the passage of the Quebec law, 83 cases have been filed regarding discrimination against this group in our community. Now, this figure is likely low because people are often scared off by the process, and, further, discrimination is often subtle and difficult to prove as being related to sexual orientation.
Some developments have also occurred in the United States. In 1982, Wisconsin became the first state to include sexual orientation in its human rights legislation. Despite some public outcry, the Governor and the majority of legislators who passed the legislation, were re-elected. People are not as scared of the issue as some would believe. American cities that have included sexual orientation in their legislation on human rights number in the hundreds. Several of the major contenders for the 1984 Presidency, including Mr. Mondale, have endorsed human rights protection for homosexuals. The U.S. Democratic Party has voted unanimously to accept the formation of an official homosexual caucus within the Party and has adopted several major pro-homosexual planks in its policy.
Perhaps the most intriguing situation is that we are starting to see some reversals in the position of individuals opposed to homosexuals and their human rights. Governor Askew of Florida who supported Anita Bryant and is reputedly seeking

May 11, 1983
Canadian Human Rights Act
the Presidential nomination, has shifted his position considerably on the issue. Anita Bryant now admits that she was wrong to campaign against homosexuals.
So we are long past the time for talking. Let us follow some of these examples. Let us send the subject matter of this Bill to committee where it can be discussed in an air of reason and where we can identify the real concerns of members of this community.

speakeroldname: Mr. A1 MacBain (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROHIBIT DISCR1MINATION ON GROUND OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) wants Parliament to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act in order to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. To this effect he has introduced Bill C-676, an Act to Amend the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Before commenting on this Bill I must mention that the human rights record of this Government is a proud one. It is responsible for the enshrinement in our Constitution of a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As a result of its endeavours, fundamental freedoms as well as democratic, mobility, legal and linguistic rights are now protected. In addition, from April 17, 1985 onwards individuals will also enjoy the protection of Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This Section provides that:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
In addition, the Government is also responsible for the Canadian Human Rights Act which Parliament enacted in 1977. The Act applies in respect of all matters falling under federal jurisdiction. It is also binding on the Crown. This means that it applies to all federal Departments, agencies and Crown corporations as well as to private businesses that are federally regulated, such as banks, airlines and railway companies.
On March 30, 1983, Parliament adopted Bill C-141, an Act to Amend the Canadian Human Rights Act and to amend certain other acts in consequence thereof. When proclaimed, the Bill will result in a significant increase of the anti-discrimination protection available at the federal level.
In addition to the Charter and the Canadian Human Rights Act, numerous federal statutes protect the civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights of Canadians. In this respect, and among others, reference can be made to Canada's reports under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
Let us now consider sexual orientation in the context of the Canadian Human Rights Act. When the House considered this Act in 1977, the question of adding sexual orientation to the list of prohibited grounds of discrimination was raised before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The Committee rejected the amendment at that time.
I would consider it obvious that it was not the intention of Parliament at that time to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. By the same token, it cannot be inferred that the Government considers sexual orientation to be a justifiable basis for denying equality.
Without condoning discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, one can wonder if the social advantages of forbidding discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation outweighs the disadvantages of such a prohibition. In 1979, the Commission conducted a survey on the public's knowledge, attitudes and practices regarding discrimination. It asked the respondents to identify possible grounds of discrimination. Of the nine main grounds identified, sexual orientation was the last. Only 1.4 per cent of persons surveyed identified it as a ground of discrimination. Further, the same survey revealed that only 0.6 per cent of the respondents ever suffered discri-mintion on this basis. As the survey reveals, while a lot is said about discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, it would appear that this practice is not as widespread as it may seem.
Whether or not to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is a question with which legislative bodies in Canada and the United States have wrestled for years. For the most part, it was decided that the negative implications of such a prohibition outweighed its advantages. Whatever may be our views on sexual orientation, it cannot be denied that a substantial number of individuals are concerned about the possible social impact of such a measure. Whether or not these concerns are well founded is not an issue here. Suffice it to say that they exist.
While I am not prepared to support the amendment of the Canadian Human Rights Act proposed by the Hon. Member for Burnaby, I do not believe that there ought to be unjustified distinction on the basis of sexual orientation. Business and Government ought to afford to everyone equal opportunity. In this respect, I would note that this is the position of the Government as regards matters which fall within its jurisdiction. For example, access to the Public Service is on the basis of merit, a concept which is foreign to distinction of any kind. This of course includes discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.
The Government is not prepared to support Bill C-676, but I would be prepared to move that the subject matter of the Bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-676, an Act to Amend the Canadian Human Rights Act be not now
read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and
the subject matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and
Legal Affairs."

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address the Bill. Before I do, I want to make very clear the manner in which I address it. My understanding of private Members' legislation is just that. It is private in the sense that any Member can raise an issue in the form of legislation in this House of Commons. There is no Party endorsation attached to Private Members' legislation.
Additionally, it has to be said that when private Members rise to speak on that legislation, they are also expressing their views rather than the endorsation by their Party. One might argue that the Parliamentary Secretary who just rose had the endorsation of his Minister to make a specific recommendation and I accept that approach. But I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all Members of the House who are here today that when I rise, I do so from a private Member's perspective.
I hope we will always preserve private Members' legislation in the House in that form.
Too often we complain in the House that private Members do not have the opportunity to exercise their good judgment on legislation but are controlled or motivated in their actions on the basis of Party position or by Party whips. All of us have complained about that from time to time.
I would hope that private Members' legislation will not fall under those types of arrangements among Parties which to some degree remove what little independence is left to the private Member in the House.
Having said that, I oppose Bill C-676. It is very difficult to oppose legislation which appears on the surface to remove discrimination. I am sure there is no one in the House who wants to be seen as wanting to discriminate, for whatever reason.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) says that it is a human rights proposition. On the surface, one can make that argument because one is obviously dealing with the rights of human beings by definition. But I think that it goes much beyond that narrow definition. If that is all it was, then I would suggest that much of the legislation which we debate in the House of Commons would not get the debate it is now receiving.
Let me be more specific. Society constantly discriminates; society constantly judges and continually discriminates between that which is right and that which is wrong. Some might argue that that is not discrimination, but rather that it is judgment. Before you can have judgment you must have the discrimination of what is right and what is wrong. While we can argue what is right and what is wrong, I would suggest that in our context, both in the British parliamentary tradition and from a Judeo-Christian background, what we are dealing with today, both historically and on the issues that I have raised, has been declared wrong by society.
Canadian Human Rights Act
Another phrase which has crept into our society to which I have had some objection is, "the moral majority". It is an American statement which seems to be the blanket condemnation of anyone who is not seen to be "with it" in terms of these modern issues. What is wrong with being moral and what is wrong with being in the majority? I ask the House what is wrong with either one? I am not discussing methodology, I am discussing the terms. I am just a little tired of people using that appellation so readily on issues which they see in the very narrow context, that if one is against it one must be either living back in the middle ages, have no concept of the modern society or, at best, has just not yet seen the light.
Historically, people who have argued these cases use another statement, that "in this day and age it is unimaginable to think anyone would still hold these views." Yes, Mr. Speaker, not only is it imaginable but I believe it is right to hold some of these views.
My argument is that that statement is too often used when a person has no actual knowledge, when they do not want to deal with the facts any longer but will deal with a person who holds the view. The attack is on the person rather than on the view itself.
Additionally, I am concerned that so much of our legislation today-and I am not trying to be condemnatory of anyone in this House-is based on secular humanism. That is the orientation of so much of our legislation, and it is very difficult to argue the question, why are you against "people"? I am not. But if you go through the annals of history and through the basis of legislation, you will find that legislation so often in these areas of moral context was based on the traditions I have already cited.
A person who has had a great influence on my thinking about private and public affairs is Wilberforce of the Clapham Society in England. Wilberforce was elected as a very young person to the British House of Commons in an age when youth was celebrated. We sometimes think that only young people today, in this day and age get elected to the House of Commons. Wilberforce was a very close and dear friend of William Pitt the younger, Prime Minister of Great Britain, I believe, at the age of 25.
Wilberforce, with a small group of people, said there were two things he wanted to change in British society. One was the slave trade. That was a discriminatory practice, but it went well beyond just simple racial discrimination. He was challenging the very bedrock of British economic life when he took on the matter of the slave trade. The opponents he had were legion and powerful.
The second thing Wilberforce said he wanted to dedicate his life to in the House was "to change British manners". If you read the journal of Wilberforce, what he meant by manners was morals. He believed sincerely that Britain was in decay because British society was losing sight of the fundamental

May 11, 1983
Canadian Human Rights Act
moral bedrock of that society. In his mind, as you read Wilber-force, there was without question a very close tie between the singular issue of abolition of slavery and the refinement of British manners or morals. I will not go through all the history. Suffice it to say Hon. Members are familiar with the story. The very criticisms which I heard again today in the House indicating that in this day and age it is passe if one still thinks there is a moral code on which society is based and that one is naive in the extreme, are the very arguments used against Wilberforce. Despite those arguments, he prevailed. Yes, he prevailed with the support of the Prime Minister who had great courage to stand against some of the very strongest forces in society. Surely today we say that they were right.
Having said that, the question must be asked, does society generally support the Bill which the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has brought before the House? We can raise all types of statistics on both sides of the issue, but to my way of thinking this is not a statistical argument. To my way of thinking it is not valid to raise the fact that the Hyslops of Toronto were defeated. That is not the argument. But I believe sincerely in my being that the general public, the vast majority of Canadians, does not support the legislation before us.
The Parliamentary Secretary raised the suggestion that there is a certain fear concerning the social impact of legislation of this type. I think I am quoting him correctly. I have no doubt that the social impact is there. The Bill restricts itself to federal jurisdiction only, but that is fairly widespread. Where do we go from there?
There was a recent case in Saskatchewan involving a teacher with a sexual orientation other than the norm which the majority of Canadians finds unacceptable. The following proposition has developed, "You cannot remove me from my teaching position because you are discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation".
The one question which we did not answer during the entire constitutional debate-and the Parliamentary Secretary raised the matter of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms-was the question of group rights. That is a great lack in the Charter of Rights. It was raised during the proceedings of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution. I, for one, am a strong advocate of group rights. People will say that that is not an acceptable concept because what we are dealing with is a Charter of Rights for individuals, therefore by extension, how can we have group rights. Society has always had fundamental groupings on which it is based, be that a community, a service organization or a church, just to name a few.
Is it discrimination if a church decides in its adherence that the public school system is teaching a humanist philosophy to which it does not want children exposed solely and wants as
well an orientation in teaching based on Judeo-Christian traditions?
Having established and paid for that school, they discover laterally that a teacher has a sexual orientation other than that which is supported by that church. They ask that teacher to leave his or her place of service. The matter is then brought before the Canadian Human Rights Commission or the Provincial Human Rights Commission. Do the adherents of that church and the supporters of that school not have the right to discriminate? Do they not have the right to have the type of teaching and teachers who adhere to the articles of faith of that church and on which that school is based? Frankly, my answer is yes, they do. I say there is a very valid reason why there are concerned people when this type of legislation comes before us, because of the social impact.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) raised the matter that Section 4 was not affirmative section. I found it rather interesting that almost at the beginning of his remarks, before I even rose to speak, he mentioned my name. I guess he knew I was going to speak. The section he referred to is defined as a section "of special programs". How do you define the words "special programs"? I am not questioning the Hon. Member's word. He might be accurate in saying that is not affirmative action, but the way I read that section, there is no doubt in my mind that affirmative action could in fact be extrapolated from those words. The problem is not his word or his intent.
What happens when this matter leaves this Parliament and is put in the hands of the Human Rights Commission? How do they interpret those words? What corrective action do they impose on the basis of those words? With all respect to the Hon. Member for Burnaby, he cannot give me an answer as to what the decision of the Human Rights Commission would be at that stage, because we do not know the basis of the case before them which will be testing this clause or, for that matter, the people sitting on that commission at that time.
Lastly, I have before me the Minutes of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs of April 26, 1983. I want to make it clear that while the Hon. Member for Burnaby indicated that the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and he had an arrangement as to how this matter would be dealt with, at page 130:19 the Minister of Justice said in terms of the substance of the Bill, and I quote him exactly:
You may recall, of course, that I opposed the substance of his proposal; but I agreed to allow it to be discussed in order to facilitate the passage of the other legislation.
He referred to the amendments to the Human Rights legislation.
May 11, 1983

So the substance, as I understand it from the Government spokesman, is opposed as well by the Government. Mr. Speaker, you or others might argue that having said these things, especially in relation to social impact, the subject matter should be brought to committee.
